sections.html:
You have three basic routes here: an agent listing, a sale on your own, or an as-is cash purchase. Each one runs into the same village and state items sooner or later. Those are the condition report, the transfer return, the last water bill and, after recent remodeling, permit sign-offs.

Menomonee Falls is a village in Waukesha County, home to 41,291 people. Roughly 74.0% of homes are lived in by their owners, and the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 was $368,000. Many buyers are therefore comparing your house with other well-kept family homes, and a clean permit history helps yours stand up.

Village rules give homeowners a lot of room to do their own projects, which means a buyer may ask who inspected the work. If you live in a one or two family home, you can handle building, indoor plumbing, heating and cooling, and most electrical jobs yourself. The service is the exception. You sign a Cautionary Statement, pull the permits and call for each inspection.

  • A contractor hired for that kind of home needs a Dwelling Contractor Certification and a Qualifier Certification from the State of Wisconsin.
  • Give the village at least 24 hours' notice before an inspection.
  • Field inspections happen between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. After-hours visits on existing permits carry an extra charge.
  • SAFEbuilt has done the village's inspections under contract since 1985.

Did you finish a basement, deck or addition yourself? Ask the Building Inspection division whether each permit has a final inspection on file. Closing a gap now is easier than answering a buyer's inspector later. For zoning or assessing, call Community Development at (262) 532-4270.

sections.h2: Assessments and the Board of Review
sections.html:
Values are set as of January 1. During a maintenance year the number carries over unless the property itself changed, and the mail brings a Notice of Changed Assessment only to owners whose value moved. If nothing arrived, your value is the same as before.

An Open Book session takes place each fall, followed by a Board of Review meeting at Village Hall. If you want to challenge a value, go in order. Speak with the assessor informally, then file a formal objection with the Board, then, as a last step, go to Waukesha County Circuit Court. Your notice of intent has to reach the Village Clerk 48 hours or more before the Board sits. The clerk's line is 262-532-4201.

The assessor does not send or collect tax bills. Direct bill questions to the Waukesha County Treasurer.

sections.h2: Water, sewer and the sewer lateral
sections.html:
Most closings split the final water and sewer charges between buyer and seller, so a separate meter reading is rarely needed. When yours will not be split, ask the Utilities Department for a final reading and bill. Staff will want the closing date and the new owner's name. The number is (262) 532-4800.

Quarterly water bills come from three billing districts, so the dates on yours may differ from the calendar. Sewage treatment is handled regionally by the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District, which serves 28 communities.

The pipe running from your house out to the village main is the lateral, and you own it. Finding it is your task too, although village records may show its path. After a backup, crews look only at whether the main is clear. A clear main puts the next call on you, to a plumber. Take photos of the damage and write down what was lost, since that record will help you answer the sewer and water questions on the condition report.

Gather these before you accept an offer, so a title company is not waiting on you.

  • The parcel number printed on your Waukesha County tax bill. It has to appear on the deed.
  • Permit and final-inspection records for work done on the house.
  • Any Notice of Changed Assessment that came from the village.
  • Water and sewer account information for the last bill.
  • If a late spouse is still on the title, form HT-110, the Termination of Decedent's Interest. The county records it for $30 together with the transfer return and a copy of the document showing the interest. This form needs no tax bill and no death certificate.

sections.h2: What Wisconsin asks of a seller
sections.html:
Under Wis. Stat. 77.22 the seller owes a transfer fee at the rate of 30 cents for every $100 of value. The Department of Revenue takes the transfer return online, and the Register of Deeds will refuse to record your deed until that return is filed.

A separate rule, Wis. Stat. 709.02, covers a house with one to four units. You owe the buyer a finished condition report no later than 10 days after the contract is accepted. Miss that window and the buyer gets 2 business days to rescind. People selling an inherited house are often excused, because a fiduciary supervised by a court who never occupied the property does not have to complete the report.

Selling to a cash buyer as-is saves you the lender appraisal and the haggling over repairs. It does not erase the report or the return.

sections.h2: Recording the deed and what it costs
sections.html:
The Waukesha County Register of Deeds records your deed. The $30 standard fee must come as a check or money order, and a transfer fee, if one applies, rides along in that same payment. Documents filed electronically come back right away. Mail in a paper deed with a stamped return envelope and plan on 2 to 3 weeks. The office answers at 262-548-7585.

Typical filings in a Menomonee Falls sale
FilingCostWhere it goes
Deed recording$30 per documentWaukesha County Register of Deeds
Termination of Decedent's Interest (HT-110)$30Waukesha County Register of Deeds
State transfer fee30 cents per $100 of valueSeller pays with the deed
Final water and sewerSplit at closingUtilities Department, (262) 532-4800

Most sellers let the title company or an attorney draft the deed and handle both filings. Confirm with them how the recording fee should be paid before closing day arrives.

sections.h2: How the sale moves from offer to closing
sections.html:
Picture the order of events. First comes an accepted offer. Within 10 days the condition report goes to the buyer. While that clock runs, you or the title company file the transfer return and settle who covers any other costs. Near closing, you ask the Utilities Department about the final bill if the closing will not divide it. Then the deed is signed, recorded and the keys change hands.

An owner-occupant who did some projects personally should add one task at the start: check the permit files. A cash buyer may take the house in its current shape, but the buyer's title company will still ask for the parcel number and recorded paperwork.

faqs.q: Can I do my own work on my house and still sell it?
faqs.a: Yes. If you live in a one or two family home, you may do your own building, indoor plumbing, heating and most electrical work after signing the Cautionary Statement, pulling permits and calling for inspections. Expect a buyer to ask whether each permit got a final inspection.

faqs.q: Who handles final water and sewer billing when I sell?
faqs.a: Call the Utilities Department at (262) 532-4800. These charges are usually split at closing, and a final reading is available if you ask. Have the closing date and the new owner's name ready.

faqs.q: Is the sewer lateral mine to fix?
faqs.a: Yes, from the house to the village main. When a backup happens, crews check the main only. If it is clear, you call a plumber.

faqs.q: What does the Waukesha County Register of Deeds charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: The standard fee is $30 per document. Pay by check or money order made out to Register of Deeds, because cash, credit and debit are refused. Any transfer fee goes in the same payment.

faqs.q: Do I need a condition report for an inherited house?
faqs.a: Not if you are a court-appointed or court-supervised fiduciary who never occupied the property. Everyone else gives the report within 10 days after the contract is accepted, as Wis. Stat. 709.02 requires.
